content: Endometritis refers to inflammation of the uterine lining, which can extend to all layers of the uterus. Normally, the uterus is aseptic, but the migration of microbes from the cervix and vagina can result in inflammation and infection. Histopathologically, endometritis is classified into two subtypes: acute endometritis and chronic endometritis (CE). Acute endometritis typically occurs after events such as abortion, childbirth, menstruation, curettage, or intrauterine device (IUD) insertion. Symptoms of acute endometritis may include fever, pelvic pain, and vaginal discharge. Histopathological examination of acute endometritis reveals numerous neutrophils within the endometrial stroma. Chronic endometritis, on the other hand, is often asymptomatic but may present with vague symptoms. It is a potential cause of infertility. Histopathological findings in chronic endometritis include the presence of plasma cells in the endometrial stroma. This condition frequently arises due to membrane rupture during childbirth and is the most common postpartum infection. Puerperal endometritis is 25 times more likely to occur in patients who have undergone cesarean sections. Most cases of postpartum endometritis are polymicrobial, involving both aerobic and anaerobic bacteria. Postpartum endometritis is caused by bacteria ascending from the lower genital tract into the cervix during labor. Common pathogens include Escherichia coli, Enterobacter species (E. agglomerans, E. cloacae, E. aerogenes), Fusobacterium necrophorum, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Lactobacillus species (L. crispatus, L. casei, L. janssenii), Mycoplasma species (M. genitalium, M. hominis), Ureaplasma urealyticum, Prevotella species (P. bivia, P. melaninogenica), Staphylococcus epidermidis, and various nondescript streptococci. Chronic endometritis may also result from infections with microorganisms such as E. coli, Streptococcus species, Staphylococcus species, Enterococcus faecalis, Proteus species, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Gardnerella vaginalis, Corynebacterium, and yeasts like Candida species and Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Acute endometritis may also be caused by sexually transmitted pathogens such as Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Risk factors for puerperal endometritis include cesarean delivery, surgical or instrumental delivery, chorioamnionitis, prolonged rupture of membranes, retained placental fragments, postpartum hemorrhage, frequent vaginal examinations, and colonization with group B streptococcus. Risk factors associated with chronic endometritis include continuous use of intrauterine contraceptive devices, prolonged menstruation, atypical uterine bleeding, fallopian tube obstruction, multiparity, abortion, bacterial vaginosis, endometrial hyperplasia, submucosal fibroids, endometriosis, endometrial osseous metaplasia, and tuberculosis. Endometritis can lead to complications such as sepsis, abscess formation, hematoma, septic pelvic thrombophlebitis, and necrotizing fasciitis. These complications may result in uterine necrosis, necessitating a hysterectomy to resolve the infection. Surgical intervention may also be required if the infection has caused a drainable fluid collection. To reduce the risk of endometritis caused by sexually transmitted diseases (STDs), patients should practice safe sex, such as using condoms, undergo routine screening, and ensure early diagnosis and treatment of suspected STDs in both themselves and their partners. Completing all prescribed treatments for STDs is essential. To minimize the risk of endometritis following cesarean sections, prophylactic antibiotics should be administered before the procedure. Additional measures to reduce genital tract infections include routine antepartum screening and treatment of group B streptococcus (GBS) and other infections, proper handwashing, adherence to aseptic techniques, limiting vaginal examinations and invasive procedures, reducing the use of episiotomies, using synthetic sutures, decreasing cesarean birth rates, promptly repairing lacerations, employing standard suture techniques, and administering prophylactic antibiotics for anal sphincter injuries. Patients should not hesitate to contact their physician if any signs of infection are observed.
